Q1.answer: Whether normalizing each input window of a forecaster with its own recent statistics (rolling-window normalization) reduces error when a series' level shifts after training, without harming accuracy when there is no shift, and how much of any benefit depends on continuing to adapt those statistics.
Q1.missing: The Introduction never states this question explicitly; it is only recoverable from the abstract and (retrospectively) the Discussion.

Q2.answer: Forecasting is used in energy systems and deployed series can change their level after training, so a normalization scheme that is robust to such shifts would matter for real deployments. However, every motivating claim is a [CITATION NEEDED] placeholder, so the importance is asserted rather than supported.
Q2.missing: No evidence, citations, or quantification of how often/how severely level shifts occur in practice.

Q3.answer: The paper does not clearly articulate a gap in prior work. It notes many normalization variants exist (uncited) but never says what they fail to do. Implicitly, the gap is that prior work has not disentangled whether shift-induced error comes from stale normalization or from model capacity — but this is only surfaced in the Discussion as 'a question we had not stated.'
Q3.missing: An explicit statement of what existing normalization approaches lack and what specific question is unanswered.

Q4.answer: They generated SynthLoad, a synthetic hourly series with daily and weekly cycles plus Gaussian noise, and injected level shifts of s in {0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8} training standard deviations. They compared three normalizations — training-statistics baseline, rolling-window normalization (RWN, statistics of the most recent 48 steps), and RWN-fixed (statistics frozen after the first 48 post-shift steps) — all using the same 64-hidden-unit MLP, same training budget, over 5 seeds, reporting MAE.
Q4.missing: Nothing major; window/budget details are terse but present.

Q5.answer: The model, hidden size, and training budget were held identical across all conditions so that differences in error could be attributed to the normalization scheme rather than to model capacity — i.e., a capacity-controlled design. RWN uses recent statistics to track the shifted level; RWN-fixed isolates the contribution of continued adaptation.
Q5.missing: No justification for the specific 48-step window (acknowledged as untuned) or for choosing an MLP over other forecasters.

Q6.answer: Three experiments: (1) a no-shift comparison of RWN vs baseline; (2) performance under level shifts s in {0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8} for baseline vs RWN (Figure 1); and (3) an ablation with RWN-fixed to test how much of RWN's gain depends on continued adaptation. All over 5 seeds, MAE reported with standard deviation.
Q6.missing: Per-shift numeric tables for s=0.2 and 0.4 are not given (only a percentage range).

Q7.answer: No shift: RWN 0.409±0.007 vs baseline 0.412±0.006 (indistinguishable). Under shift, RWN reduced MAE by 11–29% across s=0.2–0.6. At s=0.8, RWN 0.712±0.021 vs baseline 0.731±0.015 (no claimed benefit). Ablation: RWN-fixed reached 0.518 at s=0.6, recovering about two thirds of RWN's gain.
Q7.missing: Underlying MAE values for baseline and RWN at s=0.6 are not stated, so the '11–29%' range and 'two thirds' figure cannot be independently checked.

Q8.answer: In this synthetic setting, per-window (rolling) normalization removes most of the level-shift-induced error for moderate shifts at no measurable unshifted cost, and much of shift-induced error is attributable to stale normalization statistics rather than to model capacity (since capacity was held constant). Continued adaptation of the statistics accounts for roughly a third of the gain.
Q8.missing: The causal attribution is hedged ('suggest') and rests on holding capacity constant rather than varying it.

Q9.answer: It does not establish benefit at the largest shift (s=0.8), does not establish results on real data, does not test tuned windows, does not cover shift types other than level shifts, and — because capacity was held constant rather than varied — does not decisively rule out capacity as a contributor; the normalization-vs-capacity claim remains suggestive. Generalization beyond one synthetic series is unestablished.
Q9.missing: An explicit statement of external validity limits beyond the single benchmark.

Q10.answer: A capacity-controlled demonstration that per-window normalization removes most level-shift error for moderate shifts at no unshifted cost, fails at the largest shift, and depends on continued adaptation for about a third of its gain — i.e., evidence that stale normalization, not capacity, drives much of the shift-induced error in this setting.
Q10.missing: The contribution is stated only in the Discussion, not in the abstract, introduction, or conclusion.

Q11.answer: Data are synthetic (single SynthLoad series); the rolling window (48 steps) was untuned; only level shifts were studied; capacity was held constant rather than varied; no benefit at s=0.8; only one model family (MLP). The conclusion also does not carry these caveats forward.
Q11.missing: Nothing; limitations are stated, though tersely.

Q12.answer: Rolling per-window normalization fixes most of the error from moderate post-training level shifts at no cost when there is no shift, but it fails at the largest shift and about a third of its benefit comes from continuing to adapt the statistics — shown in a capacity-controlled experiment on synthetic data.
Q12.missing: The abstract and conclusion do not deliver this takeaway, so a skim-reader would not retain it.

inference_issues.claim_text: Attributes shift-induced error to normalization rather than capacity.

location.quote: Per-window normalization removes most of it for moderate shifts at no unshifted cost

inference_issues.claim_text: States a general property of per-window normalization.
inference_issues.missing_link: Only one synthetic series, one model, and one window were tested; no basis for generalizing beyond SynthLoad.

location.quote: recovering about two thirds of RWN's gain

inference_issues.claim_text: RWN-fixed recovers ~2/3 of RWN's gain at s=0.6.

location.quote: Across s = 0.2–0.6, RWN reduced MAE by 11–29%

inference_issues.claim_text: Headline improvement given as an aggregated percentage range.
inference_issues.missing_link: Per-condition means/SDs are omitted, so the reader cannot see the distribution behind the range or whether all points clear their SDs.

location.quote: so adapting the normalization cost no measurable accuracy

inference_issues.claim_text: Claims zero accuracy cost for adaptation without shift.
inference_issues.missing_link: Two overlapping means (0.409±0.007 vs 0.412±0.006) show statistical indistinguishability, which supports 'no detectable difference' but not the stronger 'cost no accuracy' framing across settings.

objective_discrepancies: The objective requires a reader to come away knowing what was tested, found, and where it stops; the abstract and conclusion convey only 'we ran/reported experiments,' so the finding and its boundary are not delivered where readers look.

The objective's central question (does per-window normalization help under shift, at what unshifted cost, and how much depends on continued adaptation) is answered in results but never posed in the introduction — the paper concedes the question 'we had not stated.'
The objective targets non-forecasting-specialist readers, but normalization practice and the SynthLoad benchmark are not explained for that audience.
